Most AI companies competing today will not exist as independent entities within 36 months.

Gartner's chief forecaster John Lovelock told CNBC this week that every AI market the firm tracks is likely to collapse into a duopoly. His reasoning is precise: compute capacity already outstrips demand, tokens and processing power are being given away through freemium models, and every player is running a last-man-standing strategy. Consolidation and takeovers among AI-dedicated neoclouds are not a possibility — they are the expected outcome.

This lands at the same moment OpenAI revised its 2026 revenue target down by $50 billion — from $70 billion to approximately $20 billion — while simultaneously raising another $30 billion at a $1.3 trillion valuation. The gap between capital deployed and revenue captured is not narrowing. It is widening.

For executives building AI strategies, the implication is structural. Vendor lock-in risk just multiplied. The providers you select today may merge, get acquired, or disappear. Your AI architecture needs to be modular enough to survive the shakeout — and your commercial agreements need exit clauses that account for market consolidation.

The companies that endure this compression will set pricing power for the next decade of enterprise AI. The strategic question is not which AI vendor to choose. It is how to build optionality into every layer of your stack before the window closes.
